name: Shackleton Crater Rim
targetRegion: Lunar South Pole (Peak of Eternal Light)
namedAfter: Sir Ernest Shackleton, Anglo-Irish Antarctic explorer famed for the Endurance expedition
illuminationProfile: Peak illumination (~86-92% annual sunlight on ridge points)
waterIcePotential: Extremely High (permanently shadowed interior trapped at <40 Kelvin)
whyNASAChose: The rim towers over 4 kilometers above the floor, capturing grazing sunlight almost continuously while shielding deep cold-traps where volatile water ice has accumulated over billions of years.
funFact: Because the Moon's axial tilt is only 1.54°, the Sun glides along the horizon here like a golden beacon. While the rim bathes in solar rays, the crater floor has not seen sunlight in over 2 billion years!
dteCommVisibility: Direct-to-Earth link oscillates between +6° and -6° elevation due to lunar libration.
contractor: NASA Artemis Program / SpaceX Starship HLS

name: Malapert A
namedAfter: Charles Malapert, 17th-century Belgian Jesuit astronomer and writer
illuminationProfile: Seasonal high illumination (~70-80% during southern summer)
waterIcePotential: Moderate to High in localized micro-cold traps
whyNASAChose: Provides a high vantage point adjacent to Mons Malapert, offering steady Earth line-of-sight and ample solar incidence while serving as the inaugural commercial lunar landing site.
funFact: Intuitive Machines' Odysseus became the first American spacecraft to touch down softly on the Moon in more than 50 years (since Apollo 17 in 1972) and the first commercial lander in history to succeed!
dteCommVisibility: High Earth elevation window with exceptional line-of-sight to NASA Deep Space Network.

name: Mons Mouton (Connecting Plateau)
namedAfter: Melba Roy Mouton, pioneering NASA African-American mathematician and Head of Computer Programming at GSFC
illuminationProfile: Broad plateau with prolonged illumination windows (~14 days)
waterIcePotential: Subsurface volatiles detectable within 1 meter drill depth
whyNASAChose: A sprawling, flat-topped lunar mountain that stands ~6 km above surrounding terrain, providing a smooth landing zone for the ice-drilling rover.
funFact: Officially named by the IAU in 2023, Mons Mouton honors Melba Mouton, who computed orbital trajectories for NASA's early Echo 1 & 2 satellites before the Apollo era!
dteCommVisibility: Unobstructed line-of-sight to Earth across the entire 14-day landing sequence.

name: Nobile Crater Rim
mission: Griffin Mission One / VIPER Payload (Target late 2026)
namedAfter: Umberto Nobile, Italian aeronautical engineer and Arctic aviation explorer
illuminationProfile: Complex rim-valley lighting with dramatic ridge-cast shadows
waterIcePotential: Very High (extensive permanently shadowed craters and micro-cold traps)
whyNASAChose: Nobile's rim features gentle slopes allowing rovers to enter and exit extreme permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) safely to sample ground ice.
funFact: Nobile Crater's topography was sculpted by collisions over 3.9 billion years ago; temperatures inside its permanent shadows hover around -248°C (-415°F) — colder than the surface of Pluto!
dteCommVisibility: Requires careful rover trajectory planning to maintain line-of-sight over the crater rim.
keyScienceGoals: Search for water ice and other volatiles
Map volatile distribution across thermal environments

name: Shackleton Connecting Ridge
mission: Blue Origin Blue Moon Pathfinder / Artemis Base Camp
targetRegion: Connecting Ridge between Shackleton and de Gerlache
namedAfter: Topographic bridge connecting Shackleton and de Gerlache craters
illuminationProfile: Ultra-prolonged sunlight; one of the highest sunlit points on the Moon
waterIcePotential: High access to adjacent Permanently Shadowed Regions
whyNASAChose: Offers an extraordinary combination of continuous solar power generation and proximity to massive volatile deposits in two deep neighboring craters.
funFact: The ridge is only a few hundred meters wide in places! Standing on it, you would look down into two dark abysses on either side with the Earth hanging motionless right on your horizon.
dteCommVisibility: Earth hovers continuously 1° to 8° above the horizon with near 100% direct line-of-sight.
keyScienceGoals: Artemis Base Camp power generation hub

name: Geographic South Pole
namedAfter: The rotational axis of the Moon
illuminationProfile: Sun never rises more than 1.54° above or below horizon year-round
waterIcePotential: Variable depending on local rim topography
whyNASAChose: The geodetic anchor point for all lunar cartography, coordinate systems, and polar stereographic projections.
funFact: At the true south pole, all lunar longitudes converge, and all directions point North! The Sun makes a 360° circle around the horizon every 29.5 Earth days.
dteCommVisibility: Earth stays within ±6.7° of the horizon due to libration.

name: Reiner Gamma (Lunar Swirl)
namedAfter: Vincenzo Renieri, 17th-century Italian mathematician and follower of Galileo
illuminationProfile: Classic equatorial day/night cycle: 14 days full sun, 14 days night
waterIcePotential: Zero (intensely heated by equatorial sun up to +120°C)
whyNASAChose: Home to the Moon's most famous 'lunar swirl' — an enigmatic bright sinuous feature associated with a localized mini-magnetosphere that shields the surface from solar wind weathering.
funFact: Reiner Gamma has no topographic height — it is completely flat like a painting on the lunar basalt! It glows bright because its localized magnetic bubble deflects dark solar wind particles.
dteCommVisibility: Earth sits permanently high in the eastern sky at ~35° to 45° elevation, delivering crystal clear DTE comms.

name: Mare Crisium (Sea of Crises)
namedAfter: Named 'Sea of Crises' in 1651 by Italian astronomer Giovanni Battista Riccioli
illuminationProfile: Equatorial: 14 Earth days continuous blinding daylight, 14 days freezing night
waterIcePotential: Negligible (target for regolith chemistry and heat flow)
whyNASAChose: A giant 555-km wide circular impact basin filled with ancient volcanic basalt, offering ideal conditions to test lunar regolith thermal properties, GNSS reception, and X-ray imaging of Earth's magnetosphere.
funFact: Mare Crisium is easily visible from Earth with the naked eye! During the Apollo 11 moonwalk, the Soviet Luna 15 probe crashed into Mare Crisium only 800 km away from Neil Armstrong.
dteCommVisibility: Earth sits steady at ~26° to 34° elevation in the western sky with continuous DTE coverage.
